requestId.description: Idempotency key bound to one Alexandria execution payload. Generated when omitted and returned with the result.

alexandria.description: Catalogued Alexandria capability invocation, mutually exclusive with url. One {provider, capability, options} object or an array of 1-10, with contracts available through firecrawl_search or firecrawl_find_tools. Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

capability.description: Capability address as returned by search or discover, e.g. "series/observations".

version.description: Optional published workflow version. Omit to use the latest version.

tools.name: mcp__dc2c4692-a6c6-4edb-8301-12e868909281__firecrawl_search
tools.description: Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`. For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`. Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Returns result groups in `data` and an operation `id`.

For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

title.description: Short snake_case identifier for this visual. Must be specific and disambiguating — if the conversation has multiple visuals, this title alone should tell you which one is being referenced (e.g. 'q4_revenue_by_product_line' not 'chart', 'oauth_login_flow' not 'diagram'). Also used as the download filename, so no spaces or special characters.

widget_code.description: SVG or HTML code to render. For SVG: raw SVG code starting with <svg> tag, must use CSS variables for colors. Example: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">...</svg>. For HTML: raw HTML content to render, do NOT include DOCTYPE, <html>, <head>, or <body> tags. Use CSS variables for theming. Keep background transparent and avoid top-level padding. Scripts are supported but execute after streaming completes.

Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application. Finder is an application like any other: clicking the desktop, the Dock, or a Finder window (including Go to Folder) requires a Finder grant. The menu bar does not, as long as the app that is frontmost is one you already have access to.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

# Applications: In the Trenches of Football Analytics (SSAC22)

## Where this applies

- Inference: A former lineman objected that a tracking-based block metric can misread a blocker coached to set vertically, who sits closer to the quarterback at contact [12:11]. When Baylor staff read offensive line grades from PFF data in recruiting grading, they could tag blocks where the prospect's coached technique differs from the grader's expectation, then check those on film before trusting the grade.
- Inference: The panel noted that a lineman's pre-snap depth off the ball changes how much space he can reach at contact (their example was 1.5 feet [35:16]). Baylor could test whether Catapult practice data plus film tags can describe a lineman's closing speed from stance to contact. The panel's source was league tracking, not GPS units, so the first job is checking whether the resolution is good enough.
- Inference: The Ravens panelist's test, "if you took this finding to the coordinator, what would you say?" [28:08], is a usable gate for any GPS or force plate finding before it goes to a position coach: if the answer is "already known" or "no action", do not send it.
- Inference: The panelists argued that no player's numbers are independent of teammates and scheme [40:52]. For recruit grades, note who played next to the prospect (a star beside him, an unusual front) before comparing him with players from other teams.

## Eric's baseline

Eric's baseline: Metric selection for force plate reporting follows an Output, Driver, Strategy framework (a Hawkin Dynamics framework adopted in practice, not Eric's own). Inference: the panel's block win rate behaves like an output metric, while the vertical set example is a strategy difference that changes how the output reads. That is an extension, not something the panel said.

Eric's baseline: the HHPR 5355 course-team material (speaker unconfirmed, Inferred) says you do not need a fancy test, you need a good coach's eye. The panelist's distrust of data alone [13:43] agrees with that, while the baseline's own Tension 3 notes Eric's SportSmith writing prefers an objective number for daily monitoring. The talk does not resolve that tension.

No direct link found for PFF grades or recruiting grading; the baseline does not cover them.

## What would have to be true

- Film review capacity to check flagged blocks, and a written definition of what counts as a "coached difference".
- For any GPS-based lineman idea: sampling rate and positional accuracy good enough to see an inch-to-foot level difference, and enough repeated practice reps per athlete.
- A way to know which teammates were on the field for the grades being compared.

## Do not apply when

- The sample is a handful of plays; the panel itself cited a 10 or 15 play sample out of over 1000 as too small to move a group-level rating [36:47].
- The grade comes from one program's scheme and will be compared with a very different scheme without adjusting.
- The panelists' own institutional views are being used as proof (ESPN's metrics, a club's preference); the talk shows no validation numbers.
- Pro tracking data is being treated as equal to college or high school data; the speaker wanted college and high school tracking but said it did not yet exist [48:27].

## First step

Pick five offensive line recruits already graded, list for each whether the film shows a non-standard coached technique, and note whether it moves the grade you would give. Keep the notes private for now.

# Applications: The Numbers Game (SSAC24)

## Where this applies

- Inference: The panel separated "what a player did" (outcome grades such as PFF) from "what he can do" (traits), and said tracking data lets analysts estimate traits such as game speed [13:15]. In Baylor recruiting grading, keep outcome grades, scout trait grades and measured athleticism as three separate columns and combine them only in a final step, so one does not leak into the others.
- Inference: One panelist said some teams look at in-game speed rather than combine times [14:15]. Baylor can run a small internal check: compare each athlete's Catapult maximum velocity in games with the same athlete's tested sprint speed, and see where they diverge.
- Inference: The panel's warning about "rushing yards over expected" (a runner's own speed gets built into the expectation, so a fast player looks average) [36:15] applies to any norm built from Baylor GPS or VALD data. Before using position-group norms, check whether an athlete's own data is inside the benchmark he is judged against.
- Inference: The panelists said hedged probabilities do not land with football decision makers, and analysts must translate to the coach's language [40:50]. For return-to-play or load flags, give the recommendation first, then one plain-language confidence statement.
- Inference: With the transfer portal giving little warning of who is coming [30:07], incoming athletes arrive with no Baylor GPS or force plate history. A short standard arrival baseline would make later comparisons possible.

## Eric's baseline

Eric's baseline: data collection is judged on cost against insight, and when the insight stops justifying the cost you stop collecting (SportSmith article, Explicit). The panel's point that analytics should cut scouts' wasted time on poor prospects [11:43] extends the same idea to evaluation workload.

Eric's baseline: favor a small number of valid, reliable, repeatable tests tied to clear KPI categories rather than an exhaustive battery (course-team material, Inferred). The panel's idea of redesigning combine drills around what predicts game performance [15:45] agrees with this.

No direct link found for PFF data, draft modeling or transfer evaluation; the baseline does not cover them.

## What would have to be true

- Enough Baylor games with usable Catapult data per athlete to compare game speed with tested speed, and a consistent testing protocol so the test side is repeatable.
- A written definition for each grade column and a rule against editing one after seeing another.
- For norms: a count of how many athletes feed each position-group benchmark.

## Do not apply when

- The data comes from pro tracking systems that Baylor does not have; the panelists mostly spoke from NFL and vendor datasets, and some are paid by those vendors or clubs, which colors their views.
- The sample is a single season or a handful of athletes; the panel itself said models work better for tackles or cornerbacks than for picking a top-eight quarterback [37:47].
- Staff are tempted to skip in-person evaluation entirely because of a model; the panel said human judgment remains in the final decision [04:05].
- A claim depends on a name or number the captions garbled (see the summary limits).

## First step

Build a one-page table for the last completed season listing, for ten football athletes, Catapult game maximum velocity next to tested sprint speed. Treat it as a private sanity check and do not circulate it.

# SSAC18: Life Behind the Curtain An Inside Look at Working NFL Front Office

## Summary

A former sports agent who became the Green Bay Packers' contract and business executive describes how an NFL front office works from the inside. He recounts building a team abroad from nothing, then explains his role as a link between long-term business planning and the urgent needs of the football side. His stories cover contract talks, the decision to draft Aaron Rodgers while holding a long-time starting quarterback, the cost of negotiating directly with players, and weighing talent against character. The talk is anecdotal: it offers no data, no model and no Q&A, and the captions are noisy.

## Key claims

- The speaker describes his job as a fulcrum between the business side, which thinks long term, and the football side, which wants answers now [08:35].
- He says he was sometimes the voice of caution toward football staff and sometimes the voice of aggression toward the business side [09:05].
- He argues every team needs someone in that role so the organization does not split into isolated structures [09:40].
- Players mostly want to know they are getting a bit more than the other guy, not a particular dollar figure [11:12]; he calls insecurity and ego dominant in the business [11:42].
- He says a free-agent signing took over a month because the team's was the only offer, so he had to keep pushing [12:12] [12:43].
- Having no owner above him gave him freedom, and he let personnel evaluators do their jobs while he did his [13:43] [14:13].
- He says combining personnel work with payroll could be called Moneyball or analytics, and he thinks the team was ahead of its time [14:43].
- He says the team did not need a second quarterback behind a starter who never missed a game, and the pick was a present-versus-future balancing act [15:47] [16:54].
- Coaches were frustrated because the player might not help for years, or ever, and the room's mantra was to trust the board [19:59] [20:30].
- He says he expects no team to let a first-round quarterback wait three years again, because of pressure from fans [23:03] [23:33].
- Negotiating directly with players, which some offered because he was a former agent, was the worst experience, and he came to see an agent as a buffer [24:33] [25:03].
- On character, he says every player is a mix of talent and character, and that more talent brings more tolerance [26:35].
- He recounts opposing a position coach who wanted to sign a player with a long record of off-field problems, winning that argument and losing others [27:06] [27:36].
- He describes forcing a coach and a player into his office to talk, with four minutes of silence, ending with no firing and no agreement that they understood each other [29:06] [29:36].

## Numbers and definitions

- Barcelona team: 80 players selected, 40 told they could not travel, built in about 10 days [02:32].
- Opening-day ticket sales of 173 in a stadium he says holds 40,000 [02:32].
- The next night, 18,000 attended, with roughly 6,000 tickets given away by his own estimate [03:33].
- Food ordered for 60 people was eaten after 20 [05:03]; the team lasted two seasons [05:03].
- Seven contracts were waiting while he tried to reach a star quarterback [10:10].
- That quarterback's deal was described as the first hundred million dollar contract in the NFL [11:12].
- Free agent contact around March 15th, signing around April 26th [12:12].
- In the 2005 draft room, he says about 19 or 20 players were rated as first-rounders [17:55].
- The choice between two quarterbacks was "51 to 49 percent" by his recollection [18:29].
- The team reached the 24th pick with one first-round-rated name on the board [20:30].
- He kept the player's agent on hold for 15 minutes [21:31], with 13 minutes elapsed in the room [22:01] and two minutes left on the clock [22:32].
- He had three cases of direct negotiation before refusing to do it again [25:03].
- A coach's line about a player being asked to win "75 street fights a day" [27:36].

## Methods and frameworks named

- The draft board with first-round ratings, and the rule to trust the board [20:30].
- A business-versus-football time-horizon split in roster and contract decisions [08:35].
- Using an agent as a buffer in contract talks [25:03].
- No quantitative model or data set is described.

## Limits and open questions

- The talk is a first-person set of stories with no data, no outcomes tracking and no comparison group, so none of it shows a method works.
- The Moneyball or analytics description of the team's approach [14:43] is the speaker's own claim; no metric or example is given.
- Probabilities such as 51 to 49 [18:29] are recollections, not documented model outputs.
- Captions are machine text and garble many names and phrases (the Barcelona opening, the agent names, the draft sequence); treat spellings as unreliable.
- The speaker had an institutional view as a team executive with no owner above him [13:43], which may not apply to teams that do have one.
- The talk touches on a former player's later criminal conviction as an example that character is hard to judge [26:04]; no process for judging character is offered.

## Q&A

- None: the speaker says he did not plan time for questions [29:36].

A former sports agent who became the Green Bay Packers' contract and business executive describes how an NFL front office works from the inside. He recounts building a team abroad from nothing, then explains his role as a link between long-term business planning and the urgent needs of the football side. His stories cover contract talks, the decision to draft Aaron Rodgers while holding a long-time starting quarterback, the cost of negotiating directly with players, and weighing talent against character. The talk is anecdotal: it offers no data, no model and no Q&A, and the captions are noisy.

- The speaker describes his job as a fulcrum between the business side, which thinks long term, and the football side, which wants answers now [08:35].
- He says he was sometimes the voice of caution toward football staff and sometimes the voice of aggression toward the business side [09:05].
- He argues every team needs someone in that role so the organization does not split into isolated structures [09:40].
- Players mostly want to know they are getting a bit more than the other guy, not a particular dollar figure [11:12]; he calls insecurity and ego dominant in the business [11:42].
- He says a free-agent signing took over a month because the team's was the only offer, so he had to keep pushing [12:12] [12:43].
- Having no owner above him gave him freedom, and he let personnel evaluators do their jobs while he did his [13:43] [14:13].

# SSAC22: In the Trenches of Football Analytics

## Summary

A moderated panel with an ESPN analyst, a former NFL offensive lineman, a Ravens analytics staffer and a Rams panelist discusses where football analytics works and where it strains. The central tension is season-long efficiency and tracking-based line grades against the on-field view that technique, coaching and teammates shape every play. The panelists describe how analysts earn trust from scouts and coaches, why grading individuals in a team game is hard, how fourth-down attitudes have shifted, and what data they want next, such as college tracking data. The captions are heavily garbled, so turn attribution and many details need checking against the video.

## Key claims

- The moderator opens by saying analytics is no longer a novelty or a rising phenomenon [01:01].
- The Rams panelist says football analytics lagged partly because revenue sharing under the cap lowers the need for innovation in small markets [02:32].
- He adds that on-field analyses are easy to copy, so teams look for edges others cannot easily reproduce [02:32] [03:02].
- The Ravens panelist says analysts and scouts process information differently but can reach the same conclusions, and that open dialogue helps when they disagree [03:33] [04:06].

- Mitch Schwartz says crude stats such as blitz rate mislead, giving examples of one team counted as a 50% blitz team and another as an 8% blitz team [06:08] [06:38].
- He prefers to study each opponent's tendencies on film, because knowing what a defender does most often matters more than his signature move [06:38] [07:08] [07:38].
- Bryan Burke describes building block identification from the separation between all players at each time step, then adding orientation and later win and loss on blocks [08:39] [09:09].
- The Rams panelist says tracking data reduces human bias in evaluation, for example liking a well-run team and discounting a mysterious one [10:09] [10:40].
- Schwartz says the ESPN line metric looked too simple (is your player between you and the quarterback at 2.5 seconds), and that a coached vertical set can make a blocker look worse on distance [11:41] [12:11] [12:41].
- He says a tackle was second in pass block wins while leading the league in sacks allowed, which he attributes partly to quarterbacks holding the ball [14:13] [14:43].
- The Ravens panelist says her view of running backs changed: value shows up in beating second-level tacklers, vision, and speed against an unblocked edge defender [15:45] [16:15] [16:45] [17:15].
- She argues run defense and pass defense merge: solid interior linemen mean fewer defenders in the box and more help in coverage [17:48] [18:23].
- Schwartz says the running game builds toughness and that tiring defensive linemen is a real but unquantified effect, and that he would not stop running with a large late lead [19:54] [21:25] [24:00].
- He says the best way to tire a defensive line is a fast-paced passing game [21:55].
- Burke says efficiency data favor passing, and that the question is how much to sacrifice for physicality, not whether the running game matters [22:56].
- A panelist notes the NFL is results-oriented while analytics focuses on process [25:32].
- The Ravens panelist says analysts must learn what coaches and scouts value, and tests a finding by asking what she would tell a coordinator [27:37] [28:08].
- She gives an example where a play's high passer rating looked like old news to senior scouts and coaches [29:12] [29:42].
- The Rams panelist says coaches are data processors without realizing it, use information differently from each other, and should be free to succeed or fail with or without analytics [30:12] [31:42] [32:44].
- He says the share of teams going for it on fourth down rose a lot, raising what counts as conservative [33:44] [34:16].
- Schwartz says tracking could show how pre-snap depth off the ball affects a lineman's reach at contact [35:16] [35:47].
- He is skeptical of ranking individual linemen from tracking data because technique and blame assignment (lineman or running back) are subjective [35:47] [36:17] [36:47] [37:17].
- A panelist defends tracking metrics as objective and rule-consistent, noting two scouts in a room will disagree [37:47] [38:19] [38:51].
- A panelist says players picked high get more chances regardless of results and suggests quantifying that [39:21] [39:52].
- The Rams panelist says defensive line results depend on who plays next to you, using examples of players who changed teams [40:52] [41:23].
- Burke says the aim is to understand interdependencies, not assign individual values, and doubts whether isolating individual plays works for paying or drafting [41:53] [42:23].
- Burke says tracking data work requires studying the sport at a deeper level and that analytics and film communities must merge [43:25] [43:55].
- The Ravens panelist wants better ways to value positions in roster construction and says left tackle pay, once about double right tackle pay, is now close to even [45:27] [45:57].
- The Rams panelist says a talented quarterback on a rookie contract has been the biggest team-building advantage [47:57].
- Burke wants college and high school tracking data to see win rates of every lineman and pass rusher [47:57] [48:27].

- The moderator recalls one NFL official in the audience at his first visit in 2012 [01:01].
- The Rams panelist cites six or seven years of analytics effort [02:02].
- Blitz-rate example: one team called a 50% blitz team versus another at 8% when counting differently [06:08] [06:38].
- Schwartz's example: an opponent likely goes inside 80% of the time and outside 20% [06:38] [07:08].

- Schwartz's hypothetical: a team passing 70% of the time with a 24-point lead [21:25].
- Roster count: 256 drafted players per year; combine attendance of about 290 other athletes [48:58] [49:30].

- Separation-based block identification and block win rates from player tracking [08:39] [09:09].
- GPS and tracking data as a reduced-bias evaluation source [10:09].
- EPA and win probability as abstractions from down, distance and score [43:25].
- A scout-analyst bridge test: what would you tell the coordinator? [28:08].
- Film study of opponent tendencies, as practised by Schwartz [06:38] [07:08].

## Limits and open questions

- The captions are heavily garbled, with turns often unlabeled, play names wrong ("Forbert"), and "combine harvesters" appearing for the combine [49:30]. Attribution of some claims to a specific panelist is a best guess.
- The captions call two panelists "players", but some of their statements sound like club staff; their roles are unverified.
- Examples (one tackle's pass block wins versus sacks, one coach's fourth-down call) are single cases, not samples.
- The first-in-history fourth-down claim and the margin of victory are garbled [31:12] and unverified.
- The panelists' views reflect their institutions (ESPN's metrics, club preferences); no validation data is shown for the block metric.
- The panel says body blows are not quantified [24:00], so those arguments rest on experience.

## Q&A

- Will tracking data change the combine, and could it go away? Rams panelist: it will not disappear, top-10 picks are unaffected, others benefit, and meaningless drills will be replaced by ones closer to game demands [49:30] [50:02].
- Have coaches used analytics more in game planning over a career? Schwartz: yes, his team gave players data on strengths and weaknesses, such as weaker third-and-long pass protection, framed as not subjective [50:32] [51:02].

# SSAC24: The Numbers Game: Football Analytics from Combines to Championships

## Summary

A panel with a Pro Football Focus product chief, a Washington Commanders football-strategy executive, an analytics executive at a sports-analytics firm (captions: "Summer Sports") and a StatsBomb moderator covers analytics in drafting, tracking data, roster depth, in-game management, college football and analytical failures. Recurring themes: draft models are only as good as the scouting input, tracking data moves evaluation from outcomes toward traits, expectation models can misassign credit, and the hardest skill is communicating probability to decision makers. They also discuss the transfer portal, NIL, and language-model tools for coaches. Panelists speak from their own employers' viewpoints.

## Key claims

- The moderator says football's complexity far exceeds chess, so decisions still come down to humans even with a data-driven approach [03:34] [04:05].
- Palazzolo says the 2018 first overall pick of Baker Mayfield was analytically driven and did not pan out, while Josh Allen, picked seventh, became the best quarterback of the generation [04:36] [05:06].
- He says Aiden Hutchinson (caption spelling) was the clear analytical favorite over the player the Jaguars chose in the top two [05:06] [05:37].
- Clement says an offensive lineman from a small college (caption: Zack Tom of Wake Forest) was rated highly by analytics, played all five line positions, was hard to sell to scouts, and became a successful starter after being drafted by Green Bay [06:08].
- Palazzolo says PFF data covers every action, and calls the grading subjective but applied objectively [07:39].
- He values a player's whole college career, early years included, plus age adjustments [08:09], and says PFF detail is especially valuable for edge, defensive line and offensive line [08:39].
- Clement says it is hard to predict pro position from college position, and trait ratings from scouts can differ from performance under coaching assignments [09:10] [09:40].
- Shen says a draft model is only as good as the scouting data fed into it, and that he values scouts' input [11:13].
- He says data can make scouts more productive, so they stop spending time on poor players, and this earns their trust [11:43].
- The moderator says teams increasingly want to insulate scouts from analytics bias, with analysts synthesizing both views afterward [12:15].
- Before tracking data, most analytics measured outcomes, even PFF grades; tracking lets analysts estimate traits such as speed and field control [13:15] [13:45].
- Examples of teams using game speed rather than combine data are named as Rams wide receivers, and one panelist says the team may not attend the combine [13:45] [14:15].
- Teams are building their own athleticism metrics from data, which matter most for late-round picks, and combine participation is declining [14:45] [15:15].
- Panelists argue combine drills can be redesigned using tracking data to see what actually predicts game performance [15:45] [16:15].
- A panelist says medical problems found around the combine are a common reason a player falls, and risk appetite is a team's call [17:16] [17:47].
- A panelist says NFL teams are never honest about injuries [18:18], and that a quarterback's difficult stretch included eight head coaches in six years [18:49].

# SSAC18: Life Behind the Curtain An Inside Look at Working NFL Front Office

## Summary

A former sports agent who became the Green Bay Packers' contract and business executive describes how an NFL front office works from the inside. He recounts building a team abroad from nothing, then explains his role as a link between long-term business planning and the urgent needs of the football side. His stories cover contract talks, the decision to draft Aaron Rodgers while holding a long-time starting quarterback, the cost of negotiating directly with players, and weighing talent against character. The talk is anecdotal: it offers no data, no model and no Q&A, and the captions are noisy.

## Key claims

- The speaker describes his job as a fulcrum between the business side, which thinks long term, and the football side, which wants answers now [08:35].
- He says he was sometimes the voice of caution toward football staff and sometimes the voice of aggression toward the business side [09:05].
- He argues every team needs someone in that role so the organization does not split into isolated structures [09:40].
- Players mostly want to know they are getting a bit more than the other guy, not a particular dollar figure [11:12]; he calls insecurity and ego dominant in the business [11:42].
- He says a free-agent signing took over a month because the team's was the only offer, so he had to keep pushing [12:12] [12:43].
- Having no owner above him gave him freedom, and he let personnel evaluators do their jobs while he did his [13:43] [14:13].
- He says combining personnel work with payroll could be called Moneyball or analytics, and he thinks the team was ahead of its time [14:43].
- He says the team did not need a second quarterback behind a starter who never missed a game, and the pick was a present-versus-future balancing act [15:47] [16:22].
- Coaches were frustrated because the player might not help for years, or ever, and the room's mantra was to trust the board [19:59] [20:30].
- He says he expects no team to let a first-round quarterback wait three years again, because of pressure from fans [23:03] [23:33].
- Negotiating directly with players, which some offered because he was a former agent, was the worst experience, and he came to see an agent as a buffer [24:33] [25:03].
- On character, he says every player is a mix of talent and character, and that more talent brings more tolerance [26:35].
- He recounts opposing a position coach who wanted to sign a player with a long record of off-field problems, winning that argument and losing others [27:06] [27:36].
- He describes forcing a coach and a player into his office to talk, with four minutes of silence, ending with no firing and no agreement that they understood each other [29:06] [29:36].

## Numbers and definitions

- Barcelona team: 80 players selected, 40 told they could not travel, built in about 10 days [02:32].
- Opening-day ticket sales of 173 in a stadium he says holds 40,000 [02:32].
- The next night, 18,000 attended, with roughly 6,000 tickets given away by his own estimate [03:33].
- Food ordered for 60 people was eaten after 20 [05:03]; the team lasted two seasons [05:03].
- Seven contracts were waiting while he tried to reach a star quarterback [10:10].
- That quarterback's deal was described as the first hundred million dollar contract in the NFL [11:12].
- Free agent contact around March 15th, signing around April 26th [12:12].
- In the 2005 draft room, he says about 19 or 20 players were rated as first-rounders [17:55].
- The choice between two quarterbacks was "51 to 49 percent" by his recollection [18:29].
- The team reached the 24th pick with one first-round-rated name on the board [20:30].
- He kept the player's agent on hold for 15 minutes [21:31], with 13 minutes elapsed in the room [22:01] and two minutes left on the clock [22:32].
- He had three cases of direct negotiation before refusing to do it again [25:03].
- A coach's line about a player being asked to win "75 street fights a day" [27:36].

## Methods and frameworks named

- The draft board with first-round ratings, and the rule to trust the board [20:30].
- A business-versus-football time-horizon split in roster and contract decisions [08:35].
- Using an agent as a buffer in contract talks [25:03].

A moderated panel with an ESPN analyst, a former NFL offensive lineman, a Ravens analytics staffer and a Rams panelist discusses where football analytics works and where it strains. The central tension is season-long efficiency and tracking-based line grades against the on-field view that technique, coaching and teammates shape every play. # SSAC24: The Numbers Game: Football Analytics from Combines to Championships

## Summary

A panel with a Pro Football Focus product chief, a Washington Commanders football-strategy executive, an analytics executive at a sports-analytics firm (captions: "Summer Sports") and a StatsBomb moderator covers analytics in drafting, tracking data, roster depth, in-game management, college football and analytical failures. Recurring themes: draft models are only as good as the scouting input, tracking data moves evaluation from outcomes toward traits, expectation models can misassign credit, and the hardest skill is communicating probability to decision makers. They also discuss the transfer portal, NIL, and language-model tools for coaches. Panelists speak from their own employers' viewpoints.
